prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength trapping concept to atomic clocks with fractional uncertainty near 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize part on B037 with Katori and Ye. The scientific case rests on a specific, identifiable idea, the magic-wavelength lattice, which cancels the light shift of the clock transition while many atoms are held in Lamb-Dicke confinement. That idea was then carried to the 10^-18 regime, has been reproduced and exceeded by independent laboratories, and underlies centimetre-scale redshift tests, bounds on varying constants, dark-matter searches and the evidence base for redefining the second. To answer the chair's question on the Statutes' discovery-or-invention criterion, the new principle is the magic-wavelength trapping of a large ensemble, which changes both the statistics and the systematic-shift budget of an optical clock. That is distinct from the comb (a frequency-measurement tool, 2005) and from control of single ions (2012). The credit also divides cleanly, with Katori for the concept and first demonstrations and Ye for taking the strontium clock to the accuracy and stability frontier and into many-body and spin-squeezed regimes. I recall my reading of the committee's task as identifying the topic and then the people responsible for the original work; for B037 the second step is defensible without strain. On the chair's factual correction, Ye was not a 2005 laureate (Hall and Hansch were), and I withdraw any framing of Ye as part of the 2005 prize; his association with the comb is a novelty question, not a bar. Regarding the pending redefinition of the second, I treat it as confirmation of maturity: the prize recognises demonstrated accuracy and independent reproduction, not a metrological convention vote.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still novelty relative to earlier AMO and precision-measurement prizes (2005, 2012, 2018, 2022, 2023, 2025); a committee could see this as another return to one community, and I have not found a way to dismiss that other than by pointing to the specific lattice concept. Second, a two-name prize leaves out NIST, PTB, SYRTE and other lattice-clock groups, and ion-clock contributors, and some of the 10^-18 records belong to groups beyond Ye's, so the citation must be narrow and the supporting text must acknowledge them. Third, if the committee judged that Ye's contribution is mainly clock-comb integration and accuracy rather than the lattice clock itself, the credit would be less clean than I describe; I think the lattice-clock record at JILA answers this, but it is a judgment, not a proof.

responses.point: Mehlig asks what new physical principle the optical lattice clock adds beyond the magic-wavelength idea, and prefers B005 (Toner, Ramaswamy, Vicsek) for its conceptual novelty, while conceding that the omission of Yuhai Tu is a real defect.
responses.response: I take the question as fair, and my answer is that the magic-wavelength idea is itself the principle: it removes the conflict between tight trapping and an unperturbed transition, which is why a many-atom clock can beat single-ion statistics without giving up systematics. That is as much a conceptual step as an engineering one. I agree that active matter is a genuinely new branch of nonequilibrium physics, but a prize that cannot name Tu, a co-author of the Toner-Tu theory, with the two-dimensional exponents still contested, is not in better shape than B037 on either credit or maturity, and by his own account no other member shares the ranking. I would not move to B005 on the present record; if the committee did go there, I would need a route that names Tu.

responses.point: Pearce, in the chair's summary and his own statement, prefers B042 for its clean chain from idea to measurement, and as an instrument builder sees more novelty in a new class of matter than in improved accuracy.
responses.response: I respect the instinct that a new class of matter is a larger discovery than a better clock, and B042 is my first alternative; I ranked it second at the opening. But two things hold me back from it. The credit gap that you and Eriksson name yourselves, Bernevig, Hughes and the late Zhang for the HgTe proposal that Molenkamp tested, is something we cannot repair later, and the 2016 topological-phases prize and the less clean quantisation of the helical edge make the experimental half weaker than the theory. Answering your question about wording: I could accept a citation tied to the Z2 prediction and the HgTe observation that says openly that the HgTe proposal and the 3D work lie outside it, but I would then want the committee to be comfortable that this is not a prize for the whole field. I am not there yet, and the credit set for B037 does not require such a compromise.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B037 for the same reasons, correcting the chair's claim about 2005, and notes that the recurring recognition of AMO and precision measurement (2005, 2012, 2018, 2022, 2023) is the strongest reservation.
responses.response: I agree with her correction and with her answer on timing. Where I would add something is on the recurrence argument: I think it is a reason to word the citation narrowly, not a reason to prefer another field. Our task is to judge a discovery or invention, not to balance subfields by year, and a lattice-clock prize does not depend on the earlier prizes for its logic. I also share her concern about the omitted groups and would ask that the committee's accompanying scientific background name Lemonde, Derevianko and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE contributions, since the citation itself cannot.

responses.point: Kroll supports B037 and asks whether Ye should be credited for the lattice clock itself or for the comb-clock integration and the accuracy frontier, noting that groups at JILA/NIST, PTB and RIKEN also hold records.
responses.response: I would credit Ye for the lattice clock realised as a precision instrument: the strontium clock at JILA, its systematic control, and the extension to spin-squeezed and many-body clocks, not for the comb. That is why my citation says invention and realisation, and not comb-based measurement. I accept his caution that some individual 10^-18 results belong to other groups, and I think that is a reason to avoid wording that claims the whole record, not a reason to widen the name list beyond what the Statutes allow.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice as a sufficiently distinct principle from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, or reads the lattice clock as incremental.
How well the citation can separate Katori's concept from Ye's realisation without implying that the whole 10^-18 programme belongs to the two names.
Whether the credit for B042 could be made defensible by a citation that explicitly excludes the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D work; if so, I would reconsider it as a competitor.
Whether B004 (solid-state femtosecond lasers) is judged too close to the 2018 and 2023 prizes; I have kept it as an alternative but may be underweighting that overlap.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B037, B042 or B004. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, and his circuit-QED work (B008) is not part of my preferred configuration or my alternatives. My transmission-electron-microscopy background is not in the area of any shortlisted preferred or alternative ID, and I have no documented tie to Katori or Ye.
